book_title: Chapter 3: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
question: How does Alphabet secure user distribution and custom AI silicon, and how does $100 of audited FY2025 revenue flow down to Operating Income and Free Cash Flow?

epigraph.quote: Great software economics hide inside distribution tolls and silicon supply chains; you only see the true unit economics when you trace both cash and depreciation.
epigraph.author: Forensic Unit-Economics Principle

web_blocks.html: Alphabet's distribution engine runs on default placement and self-serve automation. On the advertiser side, millions of small firms and global brands buy Google Ads without human sales reps. Automated tools like Performance Max dynamically place bids across Search, YouTube, Maps, and Gmail. This self-serve funnel kept Sales & Marketing lean at 7.1% of FY2025 revenue ($28,693 million) [22]. On the consumer side, Alphabet owns two massive distribution rails: Android and Chrome. It also pays Traffic Acquisition Costs (TAC) to third-party browsers, OEMs, and carriers, led by Apple for Safari and Samsung for Galaxy devices [13][18].

In FY2025, total TAC reached $59,926 million, up from $54,900 million in FY2024, or 20.3% of Google ad revenue [13]. TAC splits into two buckets with distinct economics. Distribution TAC goes to OEMs and browser partners to secure high-margin Search traffic. Network TAC goes to AdSense and AdMob publishers, where Google passes through roughly 68%–70%+ of gross ad spend. Skeptics have long flagged Apple Safari payments as a major regulatory target. Judge Amit Mehta's December 2025 judgment barred exclusive deals and capped default contracts at one year, yet it declined to ban revenue-share payments [19]. Alphabet keeps its distribution edge for now, though annual rebidding and a pending DOJ cross-appeal add renewal risk [19][20].

In Google Cloud, Thomas Kurian's team pairs direct enterprise sales with global integrators and self-serve adoption on BigQuery and Vertex AI. Meanwhile, Alphabet's hardware supply chain shifted from standard x86 servers to a custom-silicon AI stack. Five years ago, Alphabet mainly bought commodity server racks and fiber. Today, it runs a custom-silicon manufacturing program. Google co-designs its Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom under a partnership running through 2031 [15][21]. That lineup now features the 7th-generation Ironwood (TPU v7) inference chip, built at TSMC with high-bandwidth memory (HBM) [15][21]. Unlike pure GPU buyers paying Nvidia's gross-margin markup, Alphabet captures a compute-cost edge on Gemini and Cloud workloads. That edge helps Google Cloud win multi-gigawatt deals with AI labs like Anthropic [15]. Still, rapid TPU rack buildouts and third-party compute use can create near-term working-capital and margin noise [8][15].

Tracing $100 of FY2025 revenue through the audited waterfall clarifies Alphabet's unit economics [7][10][22]. Out of every $100 in sales, $40.35 covers Cost of Revenues, including TAC, YouTube creator payouts, and data center operations [13][22]. Another $22.37 pays non-depreciation operating costs and stock-based compensation across R&D, sales, and administration [22][23]. Subtracting $5.25 for depreciation leaves $32.03 in GAAP operating profit [10][24]. Adding $7.58 in gross other income and subtracting $0.18 in interest and $6.62 in taxes yields $32.81 in Net Income [25][26]. On cash flow, Alphabet generated $40.89 in operating cash per $100 of sales, spent $22.70 on CapEx, and kept $18.19 in Free Cash Flow [7].

web_blocks.takeaway: On every $100 of FY2025 revenue, Alphabet kept $32.03 in GAAP operating profit and generated $40.89 in operating cash flow—but reinvested $22.70 into CapEx, leaving $18.19 in Free Cash Flow before the even steeper 2026 CapEx ramp.

web_blocks.title: The Depreciation Lag: Why FY2025 Margins Overstate Future Compute Costs
paragraphs: Notice the gap in the FY2025 waterfall: Alphabet spent $91,447 million on CapEx ($22.70 per $100 of revenue) while recording $21,136 million in depreciation ($5.25 per $100). Servers and network gear depreciate over 4–6 years, while data center buildings run longer. That means the $91.4 billion FY2025 spend and $195B–$205B FY2026 spend will create a rising depreciation wall from 2026 through 2030.
Management flagged on the Q3 2026 call that Cloud margins face near-term pressure from higher depreciation, energy costs, and third-party compute capacity [8].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know whether a technology giant's moat is real or rented, look at two things: how it gets users to its front door, and what happens to a hundred dollars of revenue on its way to free cash flow. For Alphabet, the front door is guarded by a combination of owned platforms—Android and Chrome—and one of the largest distribution checks in corporate history: Traffic Acquisition Costs, or TAC.

On the advertiser side, Alphabet's go-to-market machine is a marvel of self-serve automation. Millions of small businesses and global brands manage their own campaigns inside Google Ads, letting Performance Max algorithms allocate bids across Search, YouTube, Maps, and Gmail. That is why Sales and Marketing consumed just 7.1 percent of revenue in 2025—28.7 billion dollars on 402.8 billion dollars of sales. You do not need an army of account executives to sell search clicks to a plumber in Dallas.

On the consumer side, however, distribution is expensive. In 2025, Alphabet paid 59.9 billion dollars in TAC, which works out to 20.3 percent of Google advertising revenue. Part of that money goes to open-web publishers on the Google Network, where Google acts like a toll-collecting clearinghouse. The rest goes to distribution partners—most famously Apple, for default placement on Safari, and device makers like Samsung. Skeptics have long argued that paying tens of billions to Apple is a vulnerability, and the Department of Justice tried to ban those payments outright. Yet when Judge Amit Mehta issued his final judgment in December 2025, he barred exclusive contracts and capped default deals at one year, but refused to ban payments completely. That means Alphabet still has to rebid every year, and the DOJ is appealing, but the distribution tollbooth remains open.

Now look at the back end of the business—the physical supply chain. Five years ago, Alphabet's supply chain meant buying standard server racks and fiber cables. Today, it is a custom-silicon manufacturing operation. Alphabet designs its own Tensor Processing Units, including the seventh-generation Ironwood TPU v7 launched in 2026 for AI inference, in a deep co-development partnership with Broadcom that stretches to 2031, with TSMC fabricating the chips. Owning the custom ASIC stack means Alphabet does not have to pay Nvidia's full hardware margin on every Gemini query or Cloud AI workload, giving Google Cloud a structural cost edge when signing multi-gigawatt deals with partners like Anthropic.

Let us walk through the audited FY2025 waterfall to see what a hundred dollars of Alphabet revenue actually produces. Out of every 100 dollars in sales, 40.35 dollars goes to Cost of Revenues—which covers TAC, YouTube creator payouts, hardware, and data center operations. Another 22.37 dollars covers non-depreciation operating expenses and stock-based compensation across R&D, sales, and administration. Subtract 5.25 dollars for depreciation of property and equipment, and Alphabet still keeps 32.03 dollars in GAAP operating profit. Add 7.58 dollars of gross non-operating income (largely equity investment gains and interest income), subtract 0.18 dollars of interest expense and 6.62 dollars of taxes, and you arrive at 32.81 dollars of Net Income.

Here is the catch you and I cannot ignore. Alphabet generated 40.89 dollars in operating cash flow per 100 dollars of revenue in 2025—a phenomenal cash machine. But it poured 22.70 dollars of that right back into capital expenditures, leaving 18.19 dollars in Free Cash Flow. And notice the accounting lag: CapEx was 22.70 dollars per hundred, while depreciation on the income statement was only 5.25 dollars per hundred. As that 91-billion-dollar 2025 CapEx bill—and the 200-billion-dollar 2026 CapEx bill—hits the depreciation schedule over the next five years, Alphabet's revenue growth will have to outrun a steeply rising non-cash cost wall. That single timing gap is why unit-economics discipline matters more for Alphabet today than at any point since its 2004 IPO.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.quote: A 40.9% operating cash flow margin is elite; the discipline test is whether $200B of annual CapEx earns its keep before the depreciation wave crests.
book_callouts.text: Every line of the FY2025 waterfall reconciles to Alphabet's audited Form 10-K. The business generates extraordinary gross cash flow, but the gap between CapEx ($91.4B) and Depreciation ($21.1B) means GAAP operating margins will face a multi-year depreciation headwind unless AI Cloud and Search revenue continue compounding at high rates.
bullets: TAC consumed 20.3% of Google ad revenue ($59.9B) in FY2025; annual 1-year rebidding under DOJ remedies introduces ongoing renewal risk.
Custom Ironwood TPU silicon co-designed with Broadcom lowers unit inference costs relative to merchant GPU-only competitors.
Every $100 of FY2025 revenue produced $40.89 in CFO, $22.70 in CapEx, and $18.19 in Free Cash Flow.
